questions.question: What are the four access modifiers in Java and what does each allow?
questions.title: Java Access Modifiers — private, default, protected, public
questions.direct_answer: Java has four access levels: **`private`** (same class only), **default/package-private** (no keyword — same package), **`protected`** (same package + subclasses in any package), and **`public`** (everywhere). They control the visibility of classes, methods, and fields and enforce **encapsulation** at compile time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of encapsulation fundamentals and how Java enforces information hiding at compile time
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing protected with default — protected crosses package boundaries through inheritance, default never does
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the least-privilege principle: always start with private and relax only when necessary, explaining the design rationale

sections.title: Access Modifiers: The Four Gatekeepers of Java Visibility
sections.content:
Access modifiers are Java's mechanism for **encapsulation** — they determine which parts of your code can see and use a class, method, or field. They are like clearance levels in a building: some areas are open to everyone (`public`), some need a department badge (default/package-private), some are for family and department (`protected`), and some are for your eyes only (`private`).

Java enforces these rules at **compile time** — invalid access won't compile. **`private`** restricts access to the declaring class. **default** (no keyword) allows access to any class in the same package. **`protected`** extends default by also allowing subclasses in other packages. **`public`** removes all restrictions. The hierarchy lets you hide implementation (the HOW) while exposing a clean interface (the WHAT).

sections.title: Four Access Levels at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|private|~Same class only|internal state|helper methods|the tightest lock
blue|default|~Same package|no keyword written|package-private|team-only API
emerald|protected|~Package + subclasses|crosses packages|via inheritance|for extension points
rose|public|~Everywhere|the official API|a permanent promise|use sparingly

sections.title: Wrong — public field lets anyone corrupt the state
Right — private field, public behavior
All Four Access Modifiers in One Class
When to Use Each Access Level
sections.content:
Use **private** for internal state and helper methods — your default 90% of the time (password hashes, internal calculations).

Use **default (package-private)** for a tightly related group of classes in one package that collaborate but shouldn't be visible outside (internal DTOs between a service and repository).

Use **protected** when designing for inheritance — fields or methods subclasses override or access (template methods, framework lifecycle hooks).

Use **public** only for the official API — methods external code should call, or widely shared constants.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing protected with default**: default is *stricter* for cross-package scenarios — protected is the one that crosses package boundaries through inheritance.
- **Making everything public for convenience**: this destroys encapsulation and couples every caller to your internals, making refactoring painful.
- **Using protected when package-private suffices**: if no subclasses exist, `protected` is overkill; default keeps the surface area smaller.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **private** — most restrictive; same class only; protects internal state.
- **default** (no keyword) — package-private; same package only.
- **protected** — same package PLUS subclasses in any package.
- **public** — least restrictive; everywhere; forms the API contract.
- **Compile-time** — Java checks access during compilation, not at runtime.
- **Least privilege** — start private and widen only when there's a clear reason.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Java has four access modifiers that control who can see and use your code. Private is the most restrictive, only the class itself can access that member. It's what you use for internal state like a password field or a helper method that's nobody else's business. Next is default, which doesn't use any keyword at all. If you don't write an access modifier, it's default. That means any class in the same package can access it, but classes in other packages can't. It's like saying this code is for our team only. Then there's protected, which is a bit tricky. It allows access from the same package, just like default, but it also lets subclasses in other packages access the member. That's the key difference, protected crosses package boundaries through inheritance, default doesn't. Finally, public is the least restrictive. Anything marked public can be accessed from anywhere in your application. You'd use public for methods that form your class's official API, the deposit method in a BankAccount class, for example. The whole point is encapsulation. You hide the how with private and default, and you expose the what with public and protected. One common mistake freshers make is thinking default allows subclass access everywhere because it sounds less restrictive than protected. Actually, default is stricter for cross-package scenarios. Another pitfall is making fields public just because it's easier, that breaks encapsulation and makes your code fragile. Start with private, then widen access only when you have a clear design reason.

questions.question: Why should class fields be private in Java, and what is the role of getters and setters?
questions.title: Private Fields with Getters and Setters in Java
questions.direct_answer: Making fields **`private`** enforces **encapsulation** — it stops external code from modifying state in unexpected ways. **Getters** give controlled read access; **setters** validate data before accepting a change. This protects data integrity and lets the internal implementation change without breaking callers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand encapsulation as a design principle, not just a syntax rule to memorize
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Generating getters and setters for every field automatically without thinking about whether each field should be mutable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention validation in setters as the real benefit, and explain that immutable fields should have getters only — no setter

sections.title: Private Fields and Accessor Methods: The Core of Encapsulation
sections.content:
Private fields with public getters and setters is the foundational **encapsulation** pattern in Java: **hide the data, expose the behavior**. A private field means the internal state is nobody's business except the object itself. You provide **getter methods** to read and **setter methods** to change — but only in ways you control.

Like a vending machine: you can't reach inside and grab items (public fields), but you press buttons and insert coins (public methods). Why it matters: **validation** (a setter rejects a negative age), **flexibility** (change how data is stored without breaking callers), and **security** (hash a password in the setter, never expose it raw).

sections.title: Encapsulation with Accessors at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Private fields|~Hide the state|no direct access|object owns its data|prevents invalid state
blue|Getter|~Controlled read|returns the value|return a copy if mutable|read-only access
emerald|Setter|~Validated write|check ranges/format|reject bad input|the real value of setters
rose|Skip accessors|~Not every field|immutable: getter only|internal cache: neither|or use a record

sections.title: Wrong — empty setter with no validation
Right — setter validates before assigning
Private Fields with Validated, Normalizing Setters
When to Use Getters and Setters
sections.content:
Use private fields with getters and setters for **mutable domain objects** where callers read or modify state but you want control — a `User` whose email is validated before acceptance.

Use **getter-only** (no setter) for **immutable fields** set once in the constructor — a `userId` or `createdAt`.

Use **neither** for truly internal data — a lazily computed cache.

Prefer **Java records** (Java 14+) for simple immutable data carriers — they generate accessors and enforce immutability automatically.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Auto-generating getters/setters for every field**: if a field shouldn't change after construction, skip the setter; if it's purely internal, skip the getter too.
- **Empty setters with no validation**: a setter that just assigns is barely better than a public field — check ranges, nulls, format.
- **Returning mutable references**: a getter returning a `List` or array lets callers mutate internal state; return `List.copyOf(...)` instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation** — private fields hide state; methods control access.
- **Validation** — the primary benefit of setters is checking new values.
- **Getter-only** — for immutable fields, provide a getter and no setter.
- **No accessors** — for internal-only data like caches.
- **Flexibility** — changing the field type won't break callers if signatures stay.
- **Records** — use them for simple immutable data carriers; defensive-copy mutable returns.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Class fields should be private because it's the foundation of encapsulation. When a field is private, only the class itself can touch it. That means external code can't reach in and set values directly, which prevents them from putting your object into an invalid state. For example, if you have a private age field, no one can set it to negative one hundred from outside the class. Instead, you provide a public setter method that validates the input. The setter checks that age is positive and in a realistic range before actually assigning the value. That's the whole point, controlled access. Getters are the read side of this pattern. They let external code see the value without being able to change it directly. So a getAge method returns the age, but callers can't modify the underlying field. This separation gives you flexibility. You could change how age is stored internally, maybe compute it from a birth date field instead, and as long as the getAge method still returns an int, no external code breaks. One mistake freshers make is auto-generating getters and setters for every single field. If a field shouldn't change after construction, like a user ID, then don't create a setter at all. Just give it a getter. Another pitfall is writing empty setters that don't validate anything. If your setter just does this dot age equals age with no checks, you've gained almost nothing over a public field. The validation is the value. Also, for immutable data like a record of query results, consider using Java records instead of manually writing all this boilerplate. Records give you automatic getters and enforce immutability, which is often exactly what you want.

questions.question: Can you use access modifiers on local variables inside a method in Java?
questions.title: Access Modifiers on Local Variables in Java
questions.direct_answer: **No** — access modifiers (`private`, `protected`, `public`) cannot be applied to local variables. Local variables are scoped to their method block and are invisible outside it anyway. Access modifiers are only for **class members** (fields, methods, constructors, nested classes) and top-level classes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise knowledge of where access modifiers apply — separates candidates who understand scope from those guessing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Attempting to declare a local variable as private or static inside a method
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that local variables are intrinsically private to the method — adding an access modifier would be redundant

sections.title: Why Local Variables Don't Need Access Modifiers
sections.content:
Access modifiers like **`private`**, **`protected`**, and **`public`** control visibility across classes, packages, and inheritance hierarchies. Local variables live inside a single method and are **intrinsically scoped** to it — born when the method starts, gone when it returns, invisible to any outside code. Applying an access modifier would be redundant, so `private int count` in a method body is a **compile error**.

Access modifiers are **only for class-level constructs**: fields, methods, constructors, nested classes, and top-level classes. Local variables, parameters, and loop/block variables are excluded because they're already isolated by **lexical scope**. The only modifiers allowed on a local variable are `final` and the `var` type inference keyword.

sections.title: Where Modifiers Apply at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Local variable|~Inside a method|block-scoped|dies at method end|already invisible outside
blue|No access modifiers|~private/public invalid|compile error|also no static|redundant anyway
emerald|Where they apply|~Class members|fields, methods|constructors, nested classes|top-level classes
rose|Allowed on locals|~Only final and var|final int x|var list = ...|not access modifiers

sections.title: Wrong — modifiers on local variables don't compile
Right — locals take only final or var
sections.content:
```java
void process() {
    int count = 0;            // valid — already private to this method
    final int LIMIT = 5;      // valid — final IS allowed on locals
    var items = java.util.List.of("a", "b"); // valid — var is allowed
}
```

sections.title: Valid vs Invalid Modifier Placement
Where Access Modifiers Actually Apply
sections.content: Use access modifiers on **class fields** (private balance, public constant), on **methods** to define your API surface, on **constructors** to control instantiation (private for a singleton), and on **nested classes** (a private static builder). **Never** use them on local variables, method parameters, or variables in loops or try-catch blocks — those are already scoped to their enclosing block.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Declaring local variables as private**: a habit from "make everything private" — the compiler rejects it because locals are already private to the method.
- **Confusing local variables with fields**: fields can and should have access modifiers; locals cannot and don't need them.
- **Using static on a local variable**: invalid syntax. For a persistent counter, declare a static field at the class level.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Local variables** — block-scoped; invisible outside the method.
- **Access modifiers invalid** — `private`/`protected`/`public` on a local is a compile error.
- **Intrinsic privacy** — locals are inherently private to the method.
- **Where modifiers apply** — fields, methods, constructors, nested classes.
- **static not allowed** — on locals; static is for class-level members.
- **Parameters** — treated like locals; no access modifiers allowed.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: No, you can't use access modifiers on local variables inside a method. Access modifiers like private, protected, and public exist to control visibility between different parts of your code, across classes, packages, and inheritance hierarchies. But local variables are already as private as they can be. They're scoped to the method they're declared in, which means they only exist during that one method execution. No code outside the method can even see them, let alone access them. So adding an access modifier would be redundant. If you try to write something like private int count inside a method, the compiler will give you a syntax error. Access modifiers are only for class members, fields, methods, constructors, and nested classes. Local variables, method parameters, and loop variables don't qualify. Think of it this way, access modifiers are for controlling who can knock on your door. Local variables are like thoughts in your head, nobody else can access them anyway, so there's no point in putting a lock on them. One mistake freshers make is trying to declare a local variable as private because they're in the habit of making everything private for security. That's a good instinct for fields, but it doesn't apply to local variables. Another confusion is trying to use static on a local variable to make it persist across method calls. That's also invalid. If you need a persistent counter, declare it as a static field at the class level, not inside the method. The only things you can put on a local variable are final, which makes it unchangeable, and var, which lets the compiler infer the type.

questions.question: What is the most restrictive and least restrictive access modifier in Java?
questions.title: Most and Least Restrictive Access Modifiers in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`private`** is the most restrictive — only the declaring class can access the member. **`public`** is the least restrictive — accessible from anywhere. The order from most to least restrictive is: **`private` → default → `protected` → `public`**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Quick recall of the access modifier ordering — straightforward but frequently asked to verify basic understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Placing protected before default in the restrictiveness order — default is actually more restrictive in cross-package scenarios
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Emphasize the principle of least privilege: start private, widen only when necessary for design reasons

sections.title: The Access Modifier Hierarchy: From Most to Least Restrictive
sections.content:
Java's four access modifiers form a clear hierarchy: **`private` → default → `protected` → `public`**. **`private`** is the tightest lock — only the declaring class, not even subclasses or same-package classes. **default** (no keyword) loosens to package level. **`protected`** adds subclasses in any package via inheritance. **`public`** removes all restrictions.

This reflects the **principle of least privilege**: start with the most restrictive access that works, then widen only with a design reason. Most instance fields should be private; API methods should be public; default and protected fill the middle for package-internal collaboration and inheritance.

sections.title: Restrictiveness Order at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|private|~Most restrictive|same class only|start here|protects internals
blue|default|~Same package|no keyword|stricter cross-package|than protected
emerald|protected|~Package + subclasses|less restrictive than default|for inheritance|crosses packages
rose|public|~Least restrictive|everywhere|the API surface|widen only with reason

sections.title: Wrong — everything public exposes secrets and state
Right — start private, widen only with reason
All Four Levels in Order
How to Apply the Hierarchy in Practice
sections.content:
Start with **private** for all fields and helper methods (password hashes, caches, internal helpers).

Move to **default (package-private)** for closely related classes collaborating in one package.

Use **protected** when designing for inheritance — subclasses in other packages need to override or read members.

Use **public** sparingly, only for the external API. Every public member is a promise you must keep, so keep the surface small.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing default and protected order**: `protected` *sounds* stricter but is less restrictive — it allows cross-package subclass access; default blocks all cross-package access. Order is private, default, protected, public.
- **Defaulting to public for convenience**: public fields let any code modify state and lock you into supporting them forever.
- **Not planning for extension**: widening a private member to protected later can be a breaking change; decide if inheritance is part of the design.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **private** — most restrictive; same class only.
- **default** — package-private; same package only.
- **protected** — same package plus subclasses in any package.
- **public** — least restrictive; everywhere.
- **Order** — private → default → protected → public.
- **Surprise** — protected is *less* restrictive than default for cross-package subclasses.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Private is the most restrictive access modifier in Java. When something is private, only the class it's declared in can access it. No other class, not even subclasses or classes in the same package, can see it. That's the tightest lock you can have. Public is the least restrictive. If something is public, any code anywhere in your application can access it. There's no restriction at all. Between those two extremes, you have default and protected. Default, which you get when you don't write any access keyword, restricts access to the same package. Any class in that package can access it, but cross-package access is blocked. Protected is the next level up. It allows same-package access just like default, but it also lets subclasses in other packages access the member through inheritance. So the order from most to least restrictive is private, then default, then protected, then public. One common mistake freshers make is thinking protected is more restrictive than default because the word sounds like you're protecting something. Actually, protected is less restrictive, it crosses package boundaries through inheritance, while default doesn't. Another pitfall is making everything public just to avoid access errors. That's convenient in the moment, but it destroys encapsulation and makes your code hard to maintain. The best practice is the principle of least privilege. Start with private for everything, then widen access only when you have a clear design reason. Most fields should be private. Public should be reserved for the methods that form your official API, the ones external code is supposed to call.

questions.question: What is the difference between protected and default (package-private) access in Java?
questions.title: protected vs default Access in Java
questions.direct_answer: **default** (no modifier) allows access only within the **same package**, regardless of inheritance. **`protected`** allows access within the same package AND from **subclasses in any package**. The key difference: `protected` crosses package boundaries through inheritance; default does not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise understanding of the protected vs default subtlety — a common interview trap question

sections.title: Protected vs Default: The Inheritance Boundary
sections.content:
The difference between **`protected`** and **default** (package-private) is one of the most misunderstood topics in Java access control. Both allow access within the same package, so they're identical when all classes share one package. The distinction only matters with **inheritance across package boundaries**.

default restricts visibility to the same package, period — even a subclass in another package cannot access a default member. `protected` extends the same-package rule to include subclasses in any package. Think of `protected` as "family and colleagues": same-package classes (colleagues) and your subclasses (family) — even across packages. That makes `protected` the **inheritance-friendly** modifier; default enforces package boundaries rigidly.

sections.title: protected vs default at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Same package|~Both allow it|default: yes|protected: yes|identical here
blue|Subclass, other package|~The real difference|default: blocked|protected: allowed|inheritance crosses
emerald|default|~Strict boundary|package cohesion|no keyword|implementation detail
rose|protected|~Inheritance-friendly|extensibility contract|family + colleagues|for base classes

sections.title: protected vs default Access Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Default (package-private) | Protected |
|---|---|---|
| Same package | Yes — all classes | Yes — all classes |
| Subclass, same package | Yes | Yes |
| Subclass, different package | No — blocked | Yes — inheritance crosses |
| Keyword | None (implicit) | `protected` |
| Design intent | Package cohesion | Inheritance / extensibility |

sections.title: Setup — a base class with both members
Cross-package subclass — protected works, default fails
When to Use Each Access Level
sections.content:
Use **default (package-private)** for a group of classes collaborating in one package with no planned inheritance — internal helpers, package-scoped DTOs. It says "this is an implementation detail of our package."

Use **protected** when designing a class hierarchy where subclasses in other packages must access fields or methods to override or extend — template methods, lifecycle hooks, configuration fields. If you aren't designing for inheritance, default is safer and keeps the surface smaller.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking default is more permissive**: default never crosses package boundaries, even for subclasses — protected is the one that does.
- **Using protected with no inheritance**: it adds surface area; someone could subclass from another package just to reach members. Use default if the class isn't meant to be extended.
- **Forgetting protected allows same-package access**: protected combines same-package and subclass access, not just the latter.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **default** — no keyword; same package only; inheritance doesn't change this.
- **protected** — same package PLUS subclasses in any package.
- **Cross-package inheritance** — protected works, default fails; the critical difference.
- **Design intent** — default for package cohesion; protected for extensibility.
- **Same package** — both behave identically there.
- **Surprise** — protected is *less* restrictive than default for cross-package subclasses.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference between protected and default access is all about inheritance across packages. Default access means you don't write any access modifier keyword at all. When a field or method is default, only classes in the same package can access it. That's true even if you have a subclass, if the subclass is in a different package, it can't access default members of its parent. Protected, on the other hand, allows access from the same package just like default does, but it also lets subclasses in other packages access the member. That's the key distinction. Protected crosses package boundaries through inheritance, default does not. Here's a concrete example. Suppose you have a class called Animal in the package com dot company dot model, and it has a default method called breathe. Now you create a subclass Dog in the package com dot company dot pets. Even though Dog extends Animal, it can't call the breathe method because breathe is default and Dog is in a different package. But if you change breathe to protected, suddenly Dog can call it because protected allows subclass access across packages. One common mistake freshers make is thinking default is more permissive because it sounds neutral or broad. Actually, default is stricter for cross-package scenarios. Another pitfall is using protected when you're not designing for inheritance at all. If no subclasses are planned, stick with default, it enforces package boundaries more tightly and prevents accidental dependencies. Inside the same package, though, default and protected behave exactly the same. The difference only shows up when inheritance crosses package boundaries.

questions.title: private vs public — Design Decision in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Private fields with public methods** is the standard OOP encapsulation pattern. Private fields hide state and prevent invalid modifications; public methods form the class's **API contract**. The design rule: hide implementation details, expose behavior through a well-defined interface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Design maturity and OOP thinking — understanding the why behind access modifiers, not just syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making fields public for convenience, creating tight coupling where every class depends on internal structure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the API contract concept: public methods are promises you make to callers; private fields let you change internals freely

sections.title: Private Fields, Public Methods: The Core OOP Design Pattern
sections.content:
The private-field, public-method pattern is the **cornerstone of object-oriented design**. Private fields hide the **internal state**; public methods expose the **behavior** — the operations clients should perform. This separates the **what** (public API) from the **how** (private implementation).

Why it matters: **data integrity** — a public `setAge` validates against negatives; **flexibility** — change internal storage (compute age from a birthDate) without breaking callers as long as the public methods stay; **maintainability** — private fields are only modified inside your class, so bugs are easy to trace. Think of the class as a **black box with buttons and displays** — clients press buttons (call methods) and read results, without touching the wiring inside.

sections.title: private vs public Design at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Private fields|~Hide the state|validate via methods|change internals freely|easy to debug
blue|Public methods|~The API contract|a promise to callers|stable interface|expose behavior
emerald|Public fields|~Only for constants|public static final|MAX_RETRIES, PI|never for mutable state
rose|Watch out|~Don't leak internals|return List.copyOf|no setter if immutable|avoid public mutable fields

sections.title: Private Fields vs Public Fields
sections.content:
| Aspect | Private fields + public methods | Public fields |
|---|---|---|
| Data validation | Enforced in setter methods | None — any value accepted |
| Implementation flexibility | Change internals freely | Changing type breaks callers |
| Encapsulation | Strong — internals hidden | None — structure exposed |
| API contract | Methods define a stable interface | Field names are the interface |
| Debugging | Changes traced to class methods | Any code can modify |

sections.title: Wrong — public mutable field leaks internal state
Right — private state, behavior + defensive copy
When to Apply Private-Public Design
sections.content:
Use private fields with public methods for **mutable domain objects** needing controlled access — a `User` whose email is validated before acceptance.

Use **private fields with no mutators** for **immutable objects** — a `Money` class or a record set once in the constructor.

Use **public fields** only for **true constants** (`public static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3`). Avoid public fields for mutable state — a public `List` lets callers bypass validation; expose a getter returning an immutable copy instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making fields public for convenience**: couples every caller to field names and types and removes validation.
- **Reflexively generating getters/setters**: skip the setter for fields set in the constructor; skip the getter for purely internal data.
- **Returning mutable references**: a getter returning the actual `List`/array lets callers break internal state; return `List.copyOf(...)`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Private fields** — hide state; prevent direct external modification.
- **Public methods** — expose behavior; form the API contract.
- **API contract** — public methods are promises; private internals can change freely.
- **Data integrity** — methods validate inputs before mutating private fields.
- **Flexibility** — refactor storage without breaking callers if signatures stay.
- **Constants** — `public static final` for true constants is acceptable.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The private versus public design decision is really about encapsulation and API contracts. The standard OOP pattern is private fields with public methods. You hide the internal state of your object by making fields private, and you expose behavior through public methods. That's the core principle, hide the how, expose the what. Here's why it matters. First, data integrity. If fields are public, any code can set them to any value, including invalid ones. If they're private with a public setter, the setter can validate the input. For example, a setAge method can check that age is never negative before actually setting the private field. Second, flexibility. If you store age as a private field but expose it through a public getAge method, you can later change the implementation, maybe compute age from a birth date field instead, and as long as getAge still returns an int, no external code breaks. But if age was a public field, changing its type or removing it would break every class that accessed it directly. Third, maintainability. When fields are private, you know all modifications happen inside your class. If there's a bug where age is set to negative one hundred, you only have to check your class's methods, not search through the entire codebase. One mistake freshers make is making fields public for convenience because it's faster than writing getters and setters. That's a short-term gain with long-term pain. Every class that touches those public fields is now tightly coupled to your internal structure. Another pitfall is auto-generating getters and setters for every field without thinking. If a field is set once in the constructor and never changes, don't create a setter. The key concept here is the API contract. Public methods are promises you make to callers. They define the stable interface of your class. Private fields are implementation details that you're free to change as long as the public methods still work.
